data_analytics.title: The Dropping Repeat-Purchase Rate
data_analytics.context: You are a Data Analyst at Nexa Mart, an online grocery delivery company operating in three cities. The leadership team is concerned about a metric that has been sliding for two quarters.
data_analytics.problem: Overall monthly orders are flat, but the repeat-purchase rate (customers who order again within 30 days) has dropped from 48% to 36% over the last two quarters. Marketing wants to know why, and what to do about it.
data_points: New customer signups are up 20% over the same period.
Average delivery time increased from 35 to 52 minutes in City B only.
Customer support tickets about 'late delivery' tripled in City B.
Cities A and C show no meaningful change in repeat-purchase rate.

questions.question: Given the data, which metric is most useful to investigate first?
options: Total signups
Repeat-purchase rate broken down by city
Number of products listed
App store rating
questions.correct_answer: Repeat-purchase rate broken down by city
questions.explanation: Since the overall metric hides city-level differences, breaking it down by city is what actually reveals where the problem lives.

questions.question: What does the data most strongly suggest is driving the drop?
options: Rising delivery times and complaints in City B specifically
A general decline in product quality everywhere
Too many new customers overwhelming the app
A citywide drop in demand for groceries
questions.correct_answer: Rising delivery times and complaints in City B specifically
questions.explanation: The delivery-time increase and complaint spike are isolated to City B, and the repeat-purchase drop pattern lines up with it - the other cities are unaffected.

questions.question: Which recommendation is best supported by this evidence?
options: Cut marketing spend in all three cities
Investigate and fix the delivery bottleneck in City B before broader changes
Launch a new loyalty program nationwide immediately
Reduce the number of products offered
questions.correct_answer: Investigate and fix the delivery bottleneck in City B before broader changes
questions.explanation: A city-specific operational problem calls for a targeted operational fix rather than a broad, unrelated change.

questions.question: Which single number would best track whether your fix is working over the next month?
options: Total app downloads
City B's average delivery time and repeat-purchase rate
Number of support staff hired
Overall company revenue
questions.correct_answer: City B's average delivery time and repeat-purchase rate
questions.explanation: The metric you track should map directly to the specific problem you diagnosed, not a broad company-wide number.

business_analysis.title: The Slow Expense-Approval Process
business_analysis.context: You are a Business Analyst at Fintrack Solutions, a mid-sized company. Employees have been complaining that expense reimbursements take too long.
business_analysis.problem: The current expense approval process takes an average of 12 business days, and employee satisfaction with the finance department has dropped. Leadership has asked you to analyze and recommend improvements.
data_points: Every expense report requires sign-off from 3 separate managers, regardless of amount.
80% of expense reports are under $50.
The finance team manually re-enters data from PDF forms into the accounting system.
Reports under $50 take just as long as reports over $1,000.

questions.question: What is the core business problem here?
options: Employees are submitting too many expenses
The approval process isn't scaled to the size/risk of each request
The company doesn't have enough managers
Employees don't understand the expense policy
questions.correct_answer: The approval process isn't scaled to the size/risk of each request
questions.explanation: Small, low-risk expenses are going through the same heavy process as large ones - that mismatch is the real issue.

questions.question: Which process change would likely have the biggest impact, based on the data?
options: Add a 4th manager to the approval chain
Create a fast-track, single-approval path for expenses under $50
Require all expenses to be submitted on paper
Remove all approval steps for every expense
questions.correct_answer: Create a fast-track, single-approval path for expenses under $50
questions.explanation: Since 80% of reports are small and take just as long as large ones, a lighter-weight path for them addresses the majority of the delay.

questions.question: Which stakeholder group's input is most important before finalizing this change?
options: Only the finance team
Finance, managers who approve expenses, and employees who submit them
Only the CEO
No one, just implement it
questions.correct_answer: Finance, managers who approve expenses, and employees who submit them
questions.explanation: A process change affects everyone who touches it - gathering input from all affected groups reduces the risk of a flawed rollout.

questions.question: Given limited time this quarter, what should be prioritized first?
options: Automating PDF data entry, since it's a smaller technical fix
The fast-track approval change, since it affects the most reports with the least risk
Redesigning the whole finance department
Nothing, wait until next year
questions.correct_answer: The fast-track approval change, since it affects the most reports with the least risk
questions.explanation: Prioritization should weigh impact against effort and risk - the fast-track change touches the most reports for a low-risk, high-value fix.

marketing.title: The Underperforming Product Launch Campaign
marketing.context: You are a Marketing Analyst at Bloom & Co, a skincare brand. The company just launched a new product with a multi-channel campaign.
marketing.problem: The campaign generated strong impressions and website traffic, but the conversion rate (visitors who purchased) is only 0.8%, well below the brand's usual 2.5% average.
data_points: Instagram ads drove 60% of traffic but converted at just 0.3%.
Email to existing customers drove 15% of traffic but converted at 4.1%.
The product landing page loads in 6 seconds on mobile (vs 2s on desktop).
70% of the traffic is from mobile devices.

questions.question: What is the core problem suggested by this data?
options: The product itself is unwanted
A likely mobile experience issue is suppressing conversions from the biggest traffic source
Email marketing doesn't work
The brand has no loyal customers
questions.correct_answer: A likely mobile experience issue is suppressing conversions from the biggest traffic source
questions.explanation: Most traffic is mobile, mobile load time is far slower, and the channel bringing the most mobile traffic (Instagram) converts worst - these point to a mobile experience problem.

questions.question: Which insight about the audience is most useful here?
options: Existing customers (email) convert far better than new cold traffic (Instagram)
Instagram users never buy anything, ever
All channels perform identically
Desktop users are the majority
questions.correct_answer: Existing customers (email) convert far better than new cold traffic (Instagram)
questions.explanation: The email segment's much higher conversion shows warmer, known customers respond very differently than cold social traffic - useful for planning next steps.

questions.question: What should be fixed first to improve the campaign fastest?
options: Increase the Instagram budget further with no other changes
Fix the mobile landing page speed, since most traffic is mobile and it's clearly underperforming
Cancel the email campaign since it has less traffic
Pause the entire campaign indefinitely
questions.correct_answer: Fix the mobile landing page speed, since most traffic is mobile and it's clearly underperforming
questions.explanation: Fixing the highest-impact bottleneck (mobile speed, affecting most of the traffic) is likely to move conversion the most, the fastest.

questions.question: Which audience segment might be worth a follow-up campaign, based on this data?
options: New cold Instagram traffic with no changes
Existing customers, since they already convert well via email
People who have never heard of the brand
Random audiences with no targeting
questions.correct_answer: Existing customers, since they already convert well via email
questions.explanation: Segments that already convert well are efficient to invest further in, while the weaker segment needs a fix before scaling spend.

finance.title: The Profitable Company Running Out of Cash
finance.context: You are a Finance Analyst at Kestrel Manufacturing. The company reported its best-ever profit last quarter, but the CFO is worried.
finance.problem: Kestrel's income statement shows a healthy $200,000 profit last quarter, but the company's cash balance dropped by $80,000 in the same period, and it may struggle to pay suppliers next month.
data_points: Accounts receivable (money owed by customers) grew by $180,000 this quarter.
The company extended payment terms for its largest client from 30 to 90 days.
Accounts payable (money owed to suppliers) stayed flat.
No large equipment purchases were made this quarter.

questions.question: What is the core issue here?
options: The company isn't actually profitable
A cash flow timing gap between reported profit and cash collected
The company spent too much on equipment
Suppliers are charging too much
questions.correct_answer: A cash flow timing gap between reported profit and cash collected
questions.explanation: Profit is an accounting figure that doesn't always match cash in hand - here, sales are booked as profit before the cash is actually collected.

questions.question: Which piece of data best explains the cash shortfall?
options: The flat accounts payable
The large increase in accounts receivable combined with extended client payment terms
The lack of equipment purchases
The overall profit figure
questions.correct_answer: The large increase in accounts receivable combined with extended client payment terms
questions.explanation: Extending payment terms means revenue is earned on paper but the cash hasn't arrived yet - exactly what the receivables increase shows.

questions.question: If receivables of $180,000 are collected over 90 days evenly, roughly how much cash should come in per month?
questions.explanation: 180,000 spread evenly over 3 months (90 days) is 180,000 / 3 = 60,000 per month.

questions.question: What is the most sound recommendation given the risk of missing supplier payments?
options: Ignore it since profit is high
Arrange short-term financing or renegotiate terms while collections catch up
Immediately stop all sales to that client
Spend the profit on new equipment right away
questions.correct_answer: Arrange short-term financing or renegotiate terms while collections catch up
questions.explanation: Bridging a temporary cash gap with short-term financing or renegotiated terms protects supplier relationships without overreacting to a timing issue.

hr.title: The Rising Turnover on the Support Team
hr.context: You are an HR Executive at Clearwave Telecom. The Customer Support department has seen unusually high resignations recently.
hr.problem: 5 of 20 support agents resigned in the last 2 months (a 25% turnover rate in that period), compared to the company's usual 4% monthly average. Leadership wants HR's assessment before approving a hiring freeze exception.
data_points: Exit interviews mention 'no clear growth path' and 'inconsistent shift schedules' most often.
Support agents' average tenure before resigning was 14 months.
The department manager changed 3 months ago.
Pay was not commonly mentioned as a reason for leaving.

questions.question: What does the exit interview data most strongly point to?
options: Pay is the main driver of turnover
Career growth and scheduling concerns, not pay, are driving the exits
Agents are leaving for random reasons with no pattern
The company should stop hiring entirely
questions.correct_answer: Career growth and scheduling concerns, not pay, are driving the exits
questions.explanation: Since pay is rarely mentioned but growth and scheduling are, the data points to non-pay factors as the main driver.

questions.question: Which factor is most useful to investigate given the timing of events?
options: The company's stock price
Whether the recent manager change affected scheduling or growth conversations
The office's location
The company logo
questions.correct_answer: Whether the recent manager change affected scheduling or growth conversations
questions.explanation: The manager change lines up closely with the turnover spike, making it a strong candidate to investigate as a contributing factor.

questions.question: What is the best first HR action?
options: Immediately replace the new manager with no investigation
Talk with current team members and the manager to understand what changed
Offer a pay raise, since that's the usual fix
Do nothing and wait for it to pass
questions.correct_answer: Talk with current team members and the manager to understand what changed
questions.explanation: Before acting on assumptions, gathering direct input from the team clarifies whether the manager change, scheduling, or growth paths need addressing.

questions.question: How should HR communicate next steps to the remaining support team?
options: Say nothing and hope they don't notice
Acknowledge the concerns raised and share what's being done about them
Blame the agents who left
Promise unrealistic changes to calm people down
questions.correct_answer: Acknowledge the concerns raised and share what's being done about them
questions.explanation: Transparent, honest communication about real concerns helps rebuild trust with the remaining team.

technology.title: The Intermittent Checkout Bug
technology.context: You are a Software Engineer at ShopLinq, an e-commerce platform. Customers have reported that checkout sometimes fails.
technology.problem: About 3% of checkout attempts fail with a generic error, but only during certain hours. The team needs to prioritize how to investigate and fix it before the upcoming sale event.
data_points: Failures cluster between 7-9 PM daily, the site's peak traffic hours.
The error logs show 'database connection timeout' as the most common message during failures.
The payment provider's status page shows no reported outages.
The database connection pool size was last changed 2 months ago, before failures started.

questions.question: What is the most likely root cause area, based on the evidence?
options: The payment provider is down
The database connection pool is likely undersized for peak traffic
Customers are entering wrong card numbers
The website's color scheme
questions.correct_answer: The database connection pool is likely undersized for peak traffic
questions.explanation: Timeouts clustering at peak hours, combined with the connection-pool change happening right before failures started, both point to the pool being the bottleneck.

questions.question: Which piece of evidence most rules out the payment provider as the cause?
options: The time of day the failures occur
The payment provider's status page showing no outages
The error message text
The connection pool change date
questions.correct_answer: The payment provider's status page showing no outages
questions.explanation: If the provider itself reports no issues, that evidence points away from it and toward something on ShopLinq's own infrastructure.

questions.question: Given the upcoming sale event, what should be prioritized first?
options: Redesigning the checkout UI
Investigating and likely increasing the database connection pool size
Switching payment providers entirely
Ignoring it since it's only 3% of attempts
questions.correct_answer: Investigating and likely increasing the database connection pool size
questions.explanation: With a traffic-heavy event approaching, fixing the most likely, highest-impact cause first reduces the risk of widespread failures under load.

questions.question: What is the best way to confirm the fix worked before the sale event?
options: Just assume it's fixed with no verification
Run a load test simulating peak traffic and monitor timeout rates
Wait for customers to complain again
Change something else unrelated instead
questions.correct_answer: Run a load test simulating peak traffic and monitor timeout rates
questions.explanation: Simulating real peak conditions before the live event is the most reliable way to verify the fix holds under load.

supply_chain.title: The Warehouse Stockout Problem
supply_chain.context: You are an Operations Analyst at Fresh Route, a regional grocery distributor. A key product keeps running out at stores before restock.
supply_chain.problem: Store managers report the store-brand yogurt is out of stock 3-4 days before each weekly delivery, causing lost sales, while a nearby warehouse consistently has yogurt sitting unused until it nears its expiration date.
data_points: Store demand for yogurt increased 30% over the last 2 months.
The reorder point for yogurt hasn't been updated in 6 months.
Delivery lead time from the warehouse is 2 days.
The warehouse holds about 3 weeks of yogurt supply at once.

questions.question: What is the core problem here?
options: The warehouse doesn't have enough yogurt overall
The reorder point hasn't kept up with rising store-level demand
Stores don't want to sell yogurt
Delivery trucks are unreliable
questions.correct_answer: The reorder point hasn't kept up with rising store-level demand
questions.explanation: Demand rose 30% but the reorder point was never adjusted, so stores are triggering restocks too late relative to actual demand.

questions.question: Which recommendation best addresses the stockouts without creating excess warehouse stock?
options: Double the warehouse's total yogurt stock with no other changes
Raise the store reorder point to reflect the new demand level and 2-day lead time
Stop selling yogurt at all stores
Reduce delivery frequency further
questions.correct_answer: Raise the store reorder point to reflect the new demand level and 2-day lead time
questions.explanation: Adjusting the reorder point to match current demand and lead time fixes the timing mismatch directly, rather than just adding more inventory everywhere.

questions.question: Why is the warehouse's unused, aging yogurt evidence of a distribution issue rather than a total-supply issue?
options: It isn't evidence of anything
It shows enough total supply exists, but it isn't reaching stores fast or often enough where it's needed
It proves the warehouse should close
It means demand is falling
questions.correct_answer: It shows enough total supply exists, but it isn't reaching stores fast or often enough where it's needed
questions.explanation: Stock sitting unused at the warehouse while stores run out shows the problem is in how and when stock moves, not how much exists overall.

questions.question: What should be prioritized first to fix this?
options: A full redesign of the entire supply chain network
Updating the reorder point for this product, since it's the direct, fast-to-implement fix
Firing the warehouse manager
Ignoring it since it's just one product
questions.correct_answer: Updating the reorder point for this product, since it's the direct, fast-to-implement fix
questions.explanation: A targeted, low-effort fix that directly addresses the diagnosed cause should come before a larger, slower redesign.

general.title: The Missed Team Deadline
general.context: You are a coordinator on a small project team at Horizon Co. The team just missed an internal deadline for the second time this quarter.
general.problem: The team missed the deadline by 4 days. Leadership wants a short summary of what happened and a plan to prevent it from happening again.
data_points: Two team members were assigned overlapping tasks without realizing it.
The team had no shared tracker showing who owned which task.
The final review step took 3 days longer than planned.
No one flagged the delay until 2 days before the deadline.

questions.question: What is the core problem behind the missed deadline?
options: The team doesn't work hard enough
A lack of clear task ownership and visibility into progress
The deadline was unrealistic from the start
The company has too many projects
questions.correct_answer: A lack of clear task ownership and visibility into progress
questions.explanation: Overlapping tasks and no shared tracker both point to unclear ownership and low visibility as the real root cause, not effort or deadline length.

questions.question: What number best represents how early the delay could have been caught, based on this data?
options: 4 days late, caught 2 days before deadline
4 days late, caught 4 days before deadline
No way to know
It was caught immediately
questions.correct_answer: 4 days late, caught 2 days before deadline
questions.explanation: The scenario states the delay wasn't flagged until 2 days before the deadline, even though the team ultimately missed it by 4 days.

questions.question: What is the best next step to prevent this from happening again?
options: Do nothing differently and hope it improves
Introduce a shared tracker and regular check-ins so issues surface earlier
Assign all future tasks to one person only
Extend every future deadline by a month
questions.correct_answer: Introduce a shared tracker and regular check-ins so issues surface earlier
questions.explanation: A shared tracker with regular check-ins directly addresses the visibility gap that let the delay go unnoticed for so long.

questions.question: How should this be communicated to leadership?
options: Hide the real cause to avoid blame
Give a clear, honest summary of what happened and the concrete fix going forward
Blame individual teammates by name
Avoid giving any explanation at all
questions.correct_answer: Give a clear, honest summary of what happened and the concrete fix going forward
questions.explanation: Clear, honest communication paired with a concrete plan builds trust, even when reporting a miss.
